rows: Count the gold for the two panels
A frame piece and a floor

think.script: Welcome to Leonardo da Vinci's workshop in Milan, more than five hundred years ago. Leonardo painted pictures and built machines, and before he painted anything, he measured it. Here are two wooden panels. One is a long, thin strip, 1 foot 6 inches long and 2 inches wide. The other is a square, 6 inches on each side. Both will be covered in gold. Each gold sheet is a square, 1 inch on every side. Bernardo thinks the long strip needs way more gold. Look at the two panels. What do you notice? What do you wonder? Look at the units, too. Write it down. Then make a guess: which panel needs more gold? Hold on to your guess, and find out your own way.

learn.label: Lesson · the Crew's ways: same units first, or split where the units change
learn.title: Find the Area: Same Unit First
learn.where: Lesson tab, top (before the Math Crew card)
learn.script:
Here's Leonardo's gold panel. It's 1 foot 5 inches long, and 3 inches wide. Each gold sheet is a 1-inch square. Before we count anything, look at the two sides. One side is in feet and inches. The other side is just in inches. They don't match — and here's the big idea for today: you can't find the area until both sides use the same unit.

So let's fix that first. We'll change the long side into inches. One foot is 12 inches. 12 inches, plus 5 more inches, makes 17 inches. Now both sides are in inches: the panel is 17 inches long and 3 inches wide.

Now we can cover it. Watch the bottom row — one sheet, two, three, all the way across. The panel is 17 inches long, so one full row is 17 sheets.

The panel is 3 inches tall, so the rows stack up: one, two, three. Three rows, and every row is the same — 17 sheets.

We don't have to count them one by one. Three rows of 17 is 17 times 3. That's the area — the squares that cover the rectangle. Length times width.

17 times 3 is 51. The area is 51 square inches, because every sheet is one square inch. 51 square inches means 51 sheets of gold.

So remember the order. First, make both sides the same unit. Then multiply length times width. And always write the area in square units.

do.label: Do · same units first, three problems (produced: Claire)
do.title: Let's Do Some Together
do.where: Lesson tab, after Leonardo's Measuring Rules

parts.label: Problem 2
parts.title: A rug: 3 yd by 2 ft
parts.body: Express the area in square feet.

do.script: Let's do a few together. Problem 1. A gold strip is 1 foot 2 inches long and 2 inches wide. How many gold sheets cover it? Are the lengths in the same units? No. One side is in feet and inches, and the other is in inches. 1 foot is 12 inches, and 2 more is 14. So the strip is 14 inches long. One row of 14 sheets. And there are 2 rows. 14 times 2 is 28. The area is 28 square inches. Problem 2. Your turn first. Pause the video and try this one. Then press play and check. A rug is 3 yards long and 2 feet wide. Find the area in square feet. 1 yard is 3 feet, so 3 yards is 9 feet. 9 times 2 is 18. The area is 18 square feet. Problem 3. Watch out for this one. A lid is 1 foot long and 7 inches wide. Someone wrote 1 times 7 is 7. The times table is right, but the units are mixed. Change 1 foot to 12 inches. 12 times 7 is 84. The area is 84 square inches. Ask it every time: are the lengths in the same units?

parts.label: The big question
parts.title: Different units?
parts.body: Put both sides in the same unit first. Then length × width.

wrap.script: Not one sheet of the Duke's gold was wasted. So, how can you find the area when the sides use different units? Change them to the same unit first, usually the smaller one, like feet to inches or yards to feet. Then multiply length times width, and write the area in square units. Next time, the Duke wants a panel that uses exactly 48 gold sheets and is 4 inches wide. How long must it be? That's Area of Rectangles, Part 2. See you in the workshop.
